final:
**The Ninth Hour**

A lake among the hills at dusk, the sun just gone down behind the far peak, so the last of the light lies in a warm band along the horizon and the ranges above it have gone to cold grey. Fog sits on the water and eats the feet of the hills; the dark near range at the left and the pale peak at the right are the only two planes, and the lake repeats them, broken by ripples. Two bare oaks, cropped by the top and bottom of the picture, stand on the near bank; at the water's edge a woman with a bundle of faggots on her shoulder waits beside her drawn-up boat, small and dark against the light, and the birds have already gone over.

It is painted in Friedrich's manner as far as the easel allowed: warm ground under lead white, a graphite underdrawing, thin films from the tubes rather than blended passages, gradations by stipple and by paint pooling, few pigments. Where it falls short of the aim: the trees read more as poles than oaks, and the lake is soft where it should be glassy — one careless glaze cost me the whole surface early on, and I rebuilt it region by region.

final:
**Evening on the Upland Lake**

An upland lake after sundown. The sun has gone down behind the hill on the right; its last light is a warm band low in the sky and along the flank of the pale peak, while mist lies on the water at the far shore with a low wooded bank showing through it. The lake is dark and quiet — the mountain sits in it upside down as a soft pale wedge, and a few long drags are all the movement there is. Two bare trees, cropped by the left edge, stand on the near bank, their fine branchlets the most delicate thing in the picture; at the water's edge a woman stands with her bundle of faggots on her shoulder and her boat drawn up beside her, not going in yet. Birds are going home. The mood is waiting.

Coming back to it, the lake and the trees were the two weaknesses I had noted, and both took far longer than they should have. The lake ended up rebuilt from scratch — a calm dark surface with the reflection carried by tone rather than by drawn ripples — and the trees were given some thousands of fine branchlets, which turned a diagram of sticks into trees, though the limbs are still visibly bars at arm's length. I also destroyed a good deal of the picture along the way by misreading `rect` as taking corners rather than a width and height, which ran several veils and mist bands off the bottom of the canvas and buried the trees, the bank and the figure until I rebuilt them.

I stopped there.

**"Evening on the Upland Lake"**

An upland lake after sundown: the sun has gone down behind the hill on the right, and its last light is a warm band low in the sky and along the flank of the pale peak. Mist lies on the water at the far shore, where a low reed bed shows through it. The lake is dark and glassy — the peak is in it upside down as a pale wedge, and a handful of long drags are all the movement there is. Two bare oaks, cropped by the left edge, stand in silhouette on the near bank, their fine branchlets the most delicate thing in the picture. At the water's edge a woman waits with her bundle of faggots on her shoulder and her boat drawn up beside her; the birds are going home.

This last stretch went into the two passages I knew were weakest. The trunks are now even silhouettes with a little bark in them — three attempts at modelling a lit flank on them all came out too light, and I stopped. The near bank, which had been a smooth olive mound the same value as the water, is now the darkest mass in the picture, quiet and mottled, with its interest at the edge in the fringe of grass. The boat's rim was knocked back so it stops shouting. It is not a finished-masterpiece landscape: the bank is empty, the limbs are still bars, and the far shore's line is straighter than I would choose.

final:
**"Evening on the Upland Lake"** (72 × 56 cm, oil on linen)

This session I went back to the one passage my last notes called weak — the far shore — and rebuilt it. The line of reeds that had been a comb is now a low broken band of wood along the far waterline, clumped and gapped, with seven bare trees standing out of it at uneven intervals; mist swallows its base and its right-hand end. Under it, in the water, is the shore's own dark grain reflected as a soft continuous band.

What it cost: two lozenge disasters that each took four days of drying and a full cover with mist paint before I could repair them. The lesson is mechanical and I have written it down — a "body" stroke is 20–60 units long, and when my masks were 90 units wide and 12 tall, one stroke covered the whole shape and its outline became the mark. Small strokes over small shapes, then merged while wet with a clean soft brush, is what actually builds a reflection.

I also spent time nearly repainting a pale streak on the right that I took for scum on the lake; measured against a grid it turned out to be the lit crest of the near bank, and I left it alone.

Left standing: the near trees' limbs are still bars at arm's length, and the bank is still empty through the middle. Both have been corrected three times now and both got worse each time.
